items.title: Making a launch plan
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A launch plan sets out what happens before, on and after the day you open to customers. Choose a realistic date, then work backwards: what must be ready (product, price, payment, legal, support), who does each task and by when. Decide who you want to tell and how: existing contacts, local people, an email list, social media, press. Prepare simple materials in advance, such as a short description, photos and a clear way to order. Plan for demand, because success needs stock and people to serve it. Afterwards, look at what worked, and thank the first customers. A launch is the start of a relationship, not a single event.

options.text: Sets out what happens before, on and after opening to customers

options.text: To list what must be ready, who does it and by when

questions.prompt: Why plan for demand as well as marketing?

options.text: Success needs stock and people to serve customers

items.title: Launch day
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Launch day is the first real test of your plan, so make it simple and controlled. Check that everything works in advance: payment, ordering, signs, the website and opening hours. Make sure each person knows their job and who to call if something fails. Tell your customers clearly where, when and how to buy. Keep a record of what happens: how many people came, what they bought, what went wrong. Be ready to fix small problems immediately and to apologise when needed. Ask first customers for honest feedback and thank them. The day is not the finish; the days after show whether the business works.

questions.prompt: What should you check before launch day?

options.text: That payment, ordering and opening arrangements all work
That the prices cannot be changed

questions.prompt: Why keep a record of what happens on launch day?

options.text: To learn what worked and what went wrong

questions.prompt: What should you do when something goes wrong on the day?

options.text: Fix it quickly and apologise to anyone affected

questions.prompt: What does launch day mainly show?

options.text: That marketing is no longer needed
That the business has succeeded for good
Whether the plan works in real conditions

items.title: Capturing enquiries
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: An enquiry is a person telling you they might buy, so never let one go missing. Make it easy to ask: a clear phone number, a short form, a booking link, a message option. Send every enquiry to one place, such as a shared inbox or simple list, and record who it was, what they want and where they came from. Reply the same day if you can, because many people buy from the first business that answers. Follow up politely if they go quiet. Where you keep personal details, say what you will use them for and only send marketing to people who agreed to receive it.

options.text: A person telling you they may want to buy
